paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend: the safest help in the world is the LORD, and everything else is just flesh. Isaiah says the Egyptians "are men, not God; their horses are flesh, not spirit" (Isaiah 31:3). Chariots look impressive, I'll give them that, but a chariot is just a fancy way of putting your trust in something that can stumble. And when the helper stumbles, the one leaning on him goes down too.

Now, the LORD isn't a backup plan sitting on the bench. Isaiah says He comes like a lion who isn't scared by a band of shepherds shouting, and He protects Jerusalem "like birds hovering overhead" (Isaiah 31:4-5). I think that's the whole point: the same LORD who warns is the One who shields. Even Assyria, a mighty empire, falls by a sword "not made by mortals" (Isaiah 31:8).

So what do we do with that? We hear the call in verse 6: "Return to the One against whom you have so blatantly rebelled." I think the invitation is the best part, because He doesn't just warn them, He calls them back. Baker, whatever you're leaning on today, a paycheck, a plan, your own two hands, the LORD is the One who can actually hold your weight (Isaiah 31:6).
